screens.title: Animator Controller: a visual state machine
screens.narratorSegment: The Animator Controller is the central organiser of animation in Unity. Conceptually, it is a state machine: each state maps to an animation clip or blend tree, and arrows between states are transitions with defined conditions. This structure lets you describe how an entity should behave over time without hard-coding every animation change. For example, a player character might have Idle, Walk, and Run states. Each state holds a clip for that motion. The Entry state points to the initial state, often Idle. States can also host sub-state machines when behavior grows more complex, but for basic movement you’ll likely work with simple top-level states. One common misconception is that the Animator alone animates movement; it does not calculate velocity or input. Instead, you supply parameters from scripts—like IsMoving or Speed—and the Animator uses those to evaluate transitions. A practical tip: name your parameters clearly and keep the number of parameters minimal. Excessive parameters make the visual graph harder to reason about. Check your Animator in Play Mode: if states do not change as expected, confirm your script updates match parameter names exactly. Can you explain why the Animator is useful even if you plan to drive some motion with code?

keyIdea.title: Animator Controller
keyIdea.text: A visual state machine that maps animation clips to states and uses transitions to control flow.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Animator Controller
Definition
A container that holds states, clips, parameters and transitions to coordinate animation behavior.
Why it matters
Using the Animator Controller keeps animation logic visible and maintainable. Designers can tune transitions without changing code, and programmers can update parameters at runtime to trigger behavior.
  • States map to clips or blend trees that contain motion data.
  • Entry state is where evaluation begins; connect it to your default state.
  • Parameters are the external inputs the controller reads to evaluate transitions.
Key Takeaway

Treat the Animator Controller as a behavior map; it decides which clip to play when prompted by parameters.

Concrete example
A PlayerAnimatorController with Idle, Walk, and Run states. Entry connects to Idle and boolean parameters drive transitions.
Common misconception
The Animator does not compute motion from physics. It plays clips and blends between them. Use scripts to supply accurate speed or input values; Animator reads them to choose states.
Check your understanding
If a state never activates, confirm parameter names, types, and whether the parameter is updated by your script while in Play Mode.

screens.title: Animation Clips: import and create
screens.narratorSegment: Animation Clips are the atomic motion data units you use in the Animator. When you import a 3D model with baked animations, Unity often creates Animation Clips automatically, each representing a named segment like Idle or Walk. Alternatively, the Animation window lets you author clips directly in Unity — useful for UI motion, props, or quick keyframe edits when external animation data is unavailable. When authoring, Unity will attach an Animator component if one is missing and create an Animator Controller for you. Clips have important import settings: Loop Time for repeatable cycles and compression options that affect performance and memory. A typical beginner mistake is forgetting to enable Loop Time for cycles; the result is a clip that plays once and then holds the final frame. Another mistake is leaving very long or uncompressed clips that tax performance. Practical workflow: import your model, review generated clips in the Project window, and confirm Loop Time for Idle and Walk. If you need to tweak timing or add small offsets, use the Animation window to create or edit a clip, then save and test in Play Mode. What clip settings will you check first when a walk cycle freezes?

keyIdea.title: Animation Clip
keyIdea.text: A single animation segment created by import or authored in the Animation window; its import settings control looping and compression.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Animation Clips
Import vs Author
Imported clips come from external tools; authored clips are created in Unity's Animation window for quick edits or UI motion.
  • Imported clips appear under the model in the Project window.
  • Author clips by selecting a GameObject and opening Window > Animation > Animation.
  • Unity may add an Animator component automatically when authoring.
Important clip settings
Loop Time must be checked for repeating cycles. Compression reduces memory and CPU cost.
Common mistake

Forgetting Loop Time causes a walk or idle cycle to stop on the last frame. Always verify loop settings for repeating animations.

Concrete example
Import a Mixamo character with Idle and Walk clips. In the Project window inspect each clip and enable Loop Time for Idle and Walk. If you want to tweak a foot plant, open the Animation window, add a keyframe, and save a new clip.
Key Takeaway

Check Loop Time for repeating cycles and compress clips when appropriate to avoid performance and memory issues.

screens.title: States and Entry: building the flow
screens.narratorSegment: A typical Animator starts at Entry and immediately moves to a default state, usually Idle. From there, transitions define how the character moves between behaviors. Setting up transitions is a sequence: place clips into states, mark an entry connection to your default state, create transitions by right-clicking a state and choosing Make Transition, then define conditions in the Inspector. For movement, you often uncheck Has Exit Time and set a small Transition Duration, for example 0.2 seconds, to allow immediate and smooth blending as input changes. The sequence matters because creating transitions before parameters exist can lead to stale conditions; create parameters first or update transitions after adding them. A concrete step-by-step: import Idle and Walk clips, create a Bool parameter named IsWalking, make Idle -> Walk with condition IsWalking == true and Walk -> Idle with IsWalking == false, and set transition durations. A common misconception is to rely on Has Exit Time for smoothness; that blocks immediate response. After you configure states and transitions, test in Play Mode to tune durations and ensure responsiveness. Which transition duration feels responsive to you during testing?

keyIdea.title: States & Entry
keyIdea.text: Entry routes to the default state; transitions with conditions and durations control how states change in response to parameters.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › States & Entry
Step-by-step
  1. Import clips and create an Animator Controller.
  2. Drag Idle and Walk clips into the Animator to form states.
  3. Create a Bool parameter named IsWalking.
  4. Make transitions: Idle → Walk (IsWalking == true), Walk → Idle (IsWalking == false).
  5. Uncheck Has Exit Time for movement transitions and set Transition Duration to ~0.2.
Example configuration
Idle → Walk: IsWalking == true, Has Exit Time unchecked, Duration 0.2. Walk → Idle: IsWalking == false, Has Exit Time unchecked.
Pitfall

If Has Exit Time remains checked, you’ll see delayed responses because transitions wait for the current clip to finish.

Key Takeaway

Set Entry → Idle, create clear parameters, and uncheck Has Exit Time for responsive movement blending.

screens.title: Parameters: types and usage
screens.narratorSegment: Parameters are variables defined in the Animator that control transitions. Unity supports four types: Float, Int, Bool, and Trigger. A Float is useful for continuous values like speed, which you might feed into a blend tree. Ints are suitable for discrete states identified by a number, such as weapon index. Bools are ideal for simple on/off checks like IsWalking. Triggers are special: they are single-use signals that fire once and then reset, useful for transient actions like Attack or Hit reactions. Choosing the correct type prevents logic errors; for example, using a Bool where you need a momentary impulse is a common mistake that leads to stuck states. Practically, name parameters clearly, create them in the Animator’s Parameters tab, and update them from scripts: SetFloat, SetInteger, SetBool, and SetTrigger. Remember optimization advice: only update parameters when their values actually change. Repeatedly setting the same float every frame is unnecessary and can cause extra internal work. Which parameter type would you choose for a sprint action that toggles while the sprint key is held? Parameters: types and usage means animator parameters are float, int, bool, and trigger. pick the type that matches the behavior: continuous, discrete, on/off, or single-use signal.. In practical terms, float, int, bool, and trigger—what to use and when. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Animator parameters are Float, Int, Bool, and Trigger. Pick the type that matches the behavior: continuous, discrete, on/off, or single-use signal.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Parameters
Parameter types
  • Float: continuous numbers like speed for blend trees.
  • Int: discrete indices or state IDs.
  • Bool: on/off toggles like IsWalking.
  • Trigger: a one-time event for attacks or reactions.
Best practices
Name parameters clearly, update them only when values change, and use triggers for single events to avoid persistent conditions. Debugging tip: watch the Animator window during Play Mode to see parameter values change live.
Misconception

Using a Bool instead of a Trigger for transient actions can lead to stuck behavior because the Bool stays true until explicitly set false.

Key Takeaway

Match parameter types to their intended use: continuous values use floats, momentary events use triggers, and toggles use bools.

screens.title: Transitions and Conditions
screens.narratorSegment: Transitions are the arrows that tell the Animator when to change states. Each transition has conditions—expressions using defined parameters—that must be true for the transition to fire. For responsive player movement, configure transitions with the right conditions and durations. For example, Idle → Walk should trigger when IsWalking is true and Walk → Idle when IsWalking is false. Uncheck Has Exit Time for those transitions so the change happens immediately once the condition is met, and then fine-tune Transition Duration to control how quickly the clips blend. Transition Duration defines the blend length as a proportion of the outgoing clip by default; use small values like 0.1–0.25 for quick responsiveness, and larger values for smoother, slower blends. Remember to avoid overly complex condition chains—keep conditions simple and predictable. Also, ensure parameters are updated reliably by your script. If a transition never fires, inspect the Conditions list, parameter types, and whether Has Exit Time is blocking the change. After setting transitions, test in Play Mode and adjust durations until the animation feels responsive to player input. What duration gives the most natural result for your character?

keyIdea.title: Transitions
keyIdea.text: Transitions use parameter-based conditions and durations to blend from one state to another; keep them simple and test responsiveness in Play Mode.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Transitions & Conditions
How to set conditions
  • Create or select a transition arrow in the Animator window.
  • In the Inspector, uncheck Has Exit Time for immediate transitions when required.
  • Add conditions: choose parameter and value that triggers the change.
  • Set Transition Duration to control blend speed.
Practical tuning
Start with 0.1–0.25 for movement transitions. Increase duration for slower, more cinematic blends when appropriate.
Common mistake

Relying on Has Exit Time for movement transitions makes controls feel unresponsive. Use it only when the full clip must finish.

Key Takeaway

Tune transition duration and conditions for responsiveness; test in Play Mode and reduce complexity where possible.

screens.title: Has Exit Time vs Immediate Transitions
screens.narratorSegment: Has Exit Time determines whether a transition waits for the current animation to reach its end before allowing the state change. This is appropriate for actions that must complete—like a death animation or a charged attack—where interrupting would look wrong. By contrast, movement animations like Idle and Walk typically need immediate responsiveness so you uncheck Has Exit Time. A misconception is that Has Exit Time makes blends smoother; it's actually a gating mechanism that prevents transitions until the clip reaches a specified point. Transition Duration controls blending, not responsiveness gating. Practically, uncheck Has Exit Time for movement transitions and tune Transition Duration to control the blend. For a death animation keep Has Exit Time checked so the sequence plays fully. During debugging, if your movement input doesn't immediately change animation, check Has Exit Time first, then parameter updates. Consider this rule of thumb: if the action must visually finish, use Has Exit Time; if player control requires immediate response, leave it unchecked. Which actions in your game should be uninterruptible? Has Exit Time vs Immediate Transitions means when checked, transitions wait for the current clip to reach its exit time; use it for uninterruptible actions and avoid it for responsive movement.. In practical terms, when to require an animation to finish and when to allow interrupting blends. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: When checked, transitions wait for the current clip to reach its exit time; use it for uninterruptible actions and avoid it for responsive movement.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Has Exit Time
Has Exit Time: When to use
  • Use for actions that must finish visually, like death or full attack sequences.
  • Do not use for movement transitions where immediate response is needed.
  • Remember: Transition Duration is separate and controls blending.
Example
An Attack state should have Has Exit Time checked if you want the attack animation to play completely before returning to Idle. Movement states like Walk should have it unchecked for responsiveness.
Key Takeaway

Use Has Exit Time to prevent interruption on critical animations. For gameplay responsiveness, prefer unchecked and tune Transition Duration for blend smoothness.

screens.title: Loop Time and clip optimization
screens.narratorSegment: Loop Time is an import property on animation clips that makes them repeat continuously. For repeating cycles like Idle or Walk you must enable Loop Time; otherwise the clip plays once and the character freezes on the last frame. This is one of the most frequent beginner mistakes. Beyond loop settings, clips should be optimized: use compression options such as keyframe reduction or Unity's optimal settings to reduce C P U and memory usage. Long, uncompressed clips consume more resources, and many complex animators across many GameObjects can add up. Another optimization is to avoid unnecessary parameter updates in scripts. Only set Animator parameters when values change—this reduces internal work. For example, cache the previous speed and only call SetFloat when the new speed differs by a threshold. Finally, test in a build or with profiling tools if you suspect animation is the bottleneck. If performance is acceptable in the Editor but drops in a build, re-evaluate clip lengths and compression settings. What threshold will you use before calling SetFloat again in your project? Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › PlayerAnimatorController
C# Example (starter)
using UnityEngine;

public class PlayerAnimatorController : MonoBehaviour
{
    [SerializeField] private Animator animator;
    [SerializeField] private float moveSpeedThreshold = 0.1f;
    [SerializeField] private float runSpeedThreshold = 3.0f; // Example threshold

    private CharacterController characterController;

    void Start()
    {
        if (animator == null)
        {
            animator = GetComponent<Animator>();
            if (animator == null)
            {
                Debug.LogError("Animator component not found on this GameObject.", this);
                enabled = false;
                return;
            }
        }
        characterController = GetComponent<CharacterController>();
    }

    void Update()
    {
        float currentSpeed = 0f;
        if (characterController != null)
        {
            Vector3 horizontalVelocity = characterController.velocity;
            horizontalVelocity.y = 0;
            currentSpeed = horizontalVelocity.magnitude;
        }
        else
        {
            currentSpeed = Input.GetAxis("Horizontal") != 0 || Input.GetAxis("Vertical") != 0 ? 1.0f : 0f;
            if (Input.GetKey(KeyCode.LeftShift)) currentSpeed *= 2.0f;
        }

        bool isMoving = currentSpeed > moveSpeedThreshold;
        bool isRunning = currentSpeed > runSpeedThreshold;

        animator.SetBool("IsMoving", isMoving);
        animator.SetBool("IsRunning", isRunning);
        animator.SetFloat("Speed", currentSpeed);
    }
}
Explanation
  • Start: ensure Animator exists and cache components.
  • Update: compute horizontal speed and derive booleans.
  • Set Animator parameters to drive transitions and blend trees.
Pro tip: compare previousSpeed to currentSpeed and only call SetFloat when the difference exceeds a small epsilon to reduce updates.
Key Takeaway

Use defensive checks, compute local horizontal speed, and update Animator parameters only when values meaningfully change.

screens.title: Common animation issues and how to fix them
screens.narratorSegment: Troubleshooting animation issues is largely about checking a short list of likely causes. If a clip plays once and then freezes on the last frame, the most likely cause is Loop Time being unchecked on that clip. Open the clip’s import settings and enable Loop Time. If transitions are delayed, check whether Has Exit Time is enabled on the transition. For movement controls you usually want it unchecked. If a state never activates, confirm the parameter exists, has the correct type, and your script updates it with the exact name. A frequent scripting error is repeatedly setting the same parameter value every frame; instead, update only when values change to reduce overhead. If multiple animators exist, ensure the correct Animator is referenced in your script; missing Animator references can silently disable animation updates. For performance problems, review clip lengths and compression settings and avoid using uncompressed, long clips across many characters. Finally, use Play Mode with the Animator window open to watch parameters and state changes live—this is often the fastest way to identify mismatches between expected and actual behavior. fullNarratorScript:
Animation brings your game world to life. In Unity, animation is managed by the Animator Controller, a visual state machine that ties animation clips to named states and governs transitions using parameters. In this chapter you will learn what an Animator Controller is, how animation clips are created or imported, how states and transitions work, and how to drive animations from C# scripts for responsive character movement. We will also cover common beginner mistakes—like leaving 'Has Exit Time' on movement transitions or forgetting to enable loop time for continuous cycles—and practical performance tips such as compressing clips and avoiding unnecessary parameter updates. By the end you will be able to create Idle and Walk states, set up a simple IsWalking boolean parameter, configure responsive transitions, and attach a script to update those parameters from player input. A short hands-on activity walks you through importing a model, making an Animator Controller, and testing the character in Play Mode. Keep an eye out for the common mistake checks and the troubleshooting checklist; they’ll save you iterations in Play Mode. Ready to explore the building blocks of animation? Let’s begin.

These four objectives give you actionable outcomes. First, you will understand core components of Unity's animation system: Animator Controllers, Animation Clips, and States. That knowledge helps you read and modify existing controllers and build new ones. Second, you will create and manage animation clips both from imported models and inside Unity's Animation window. Practically, this means you can import a model with baked clips or author a simple UI animation right in the editor. Third, you will configure transitions between states by using parameters and conditions. You’ll learn parameter types like float, int, bool, and trigger and why each matters for gameplay responsiveness. Fourth, you will implement basic player movement animations—Idle, Walk, Run—by wiring Animator parameters to a script. Each objective contains a small mnemonic or micro-check so you can verify competency quickly. Together these outcomes let you set up a simple, responsive animation pipeline and avoid common beginner traps like leaving Has Exit Time on movement transitions. After completing these objectives, you’ll be ready to build and test character animation behaviors in Play Mode with confidence.

These follow-up objectives focus on practical skills: configuring transitions precisely, troubleshooting common animation issues, and keeping animations performant. You will learn how to set transition conditions such as 'IsWalking' or 'IsRunning' and why unchecking Has Exit Time matters for responsive input. We’ll show the specific case where Has Exit Time should remain checked—when an animation must finish, like a death or attack sequence—and why it’s inappropriate for continuous movement cycles. Next, you will learn troubleshooting steps: verify Loop Time is enabled for repeating cycles, confirm Animator parameters are correctly named and updated, and test transitions in Play Mode while observing Blend values. Finally, you will adopt basic optimization practices: compress clips via import settings and avoid redundant Animator parameter updates in Update loops. These practices improve runtime performance and reduce unexpected animation stalls. Each description includes a micro-mnemonic and a verification step so you can validate behavior in Play Mode before moving on to more advanced techniques.

The Animator Controller is the central organiser of animation in Unity. Conceptually, it is a state machine: each state maps to an animation clip or blend tree, and arrows between states are transitions with defined conditions. This structure lets you describe how an entity should behave over time without hard-coding every animation change. For example, a player character might have Idle, Walk, and Run states. Each state holds a clip for that motion. The Entry state points to the initial state, often Idle. States can also host sub-state machines when behavior grows more complex, but for basic movement you’ll likely work with simple top-level states. One common misconception is that the Animator alone animates movement; it does not calculate velocity or input. Instead, you supply parameters from scripts—like IsMoving or Speed—and the Animator uses those to evaluate transitions. A practical tip: name your parameters clearly and keep the number of parameters minimal. Excessive parameters make the visual graph harder to reason about. Check your Animator in Play Mode: if states do not change as expected, confirm your script updates match parameter names exactly. Can you explain why the Animator is useful even if you plan to drive some motion with code?

Animation Clips are the atomic motion data units you use in the Animator. When you import a 3D model with baked animations, Unity often creates Animation Clips automatically, each representing a named segment like Idle or Walk. Alternatively, the Animation window lets you author clips directly in Unity — useful for UI motion, props, or quick keyframe edits when external animation data is unavailable. When authoring, Unity will attach an Animator component if one is missing and create an Animator Controller for you. Clips have important import settings: Loop Time for repeatable cycles and compression options that affect performance and memory. A typical beginner mistake is forgetting to enable Loop Time for cycles; the result is a clip that plays once and then holds the final frame. Another mistake is leaving very long or uncompressed clips that tax performance. Practical workflow: import your model, review generated clips in the Project window, and confirm Loop Time for Idle and Walk. If you need to tweak timing or add small offsets, use the Animation window to create or edit a clip, then save and test in Play Mode. What clip settings will you check first when a walk cycle freezes?

A typical Animator starts at Entry and immediately moves to a default state, usually Idle. From there, transitions define how the character moves between behaviors. Setting up transitions is a sequence: place clips into states, mark an entry connection to your default state, create transitions by right-clicking a state and choosing Make Transition, then define conditions in the Inspector. For movement, you often uncheck Has Exit Time and set a small Transition Duration, for example 0.2 seconds, to allow immediate and smooth blending as input changes. The sequence matters because creating transitions before parameters exist can lead to stale conditions; create parameters first or update transitions after adding them. A concrete step-by-step: import Idle and Walk clips, create a Bool parameter named IsWalking, make Idle -> Walk with condition IsWalking == true and Walk -> Idle with IsWalking == false, and set transition durations. A common misconception is to rely on Has Exit Time for smoothness; that blocks immediate response. After you configure states and transitions, test in Play Mode to tune durations and ensure responsiveness. Which transition duration feels responsive to you during testing?

Parameters are variables defined in the Animator that control transitions. Unity supports four types: Float, Int, Bool, and Trigger. A Float is useful for continuous values like speed, which you might feed into a blend tree. Ints are suitable for discrete states identified by a number, such as weapon index. Bools are ideal for simple on/off checks like IsWalking. Triggers are special: they are single-use signals that fire once and then reset, useful for transient actions like Attack or Hit reactions. Choosing the correct type prevents logic errors; for example, using a Bool where you need a momentary impulse is a common mistake that leads to stuck states. Practically, name parameters clearly, create them in the Animator’s Parameters tab, and update them from scripts: SetFloat, SetInteger, SetBool, and SetTrigger. Remember optimization advice: only update parameters when their values actually change. Repeatedly setting the same float every frame is unnecessary and can cause extra internal work. Which parameter type would you choose for a sprint action that toggles while the sprint key is held? Transitions are the arrows that tell the Animator when to change states. Each transition has conditions—expressions using defined parameters—that must be true for the transition to fire. For responsive player movement, configure transitions with the right conditions and durations. For example, Idle → Walk should trigger when IsWalking is true and Walk → Idle when IsWalking is false. Seventh, ensure both clips have Loop Time enabled in their import settings. Eighth, add the PlayerAnimationHandler script to the character, and run Play Mode. Press movement keys and verify the Animator responds. If the animation does not loop, check Loop Time; if transitions feel delayed, check Has Exit Time. Troubleshooting animation issues is largely about checking a short list of likely causes. If a clip plays once and then freezes on the last frame, the most likely cause is Loop Time being unchecked on that clip. Open the clip’s import settings and enable Loop Time. If transitions are delayed, check whether Has Exit Time is enabled on the transition. For movement controls you usually want it unchecked. If a state never activates, confirm the parameter exists, has the correct type, and your script updates it with the exact name. A frequent scripting error is repeatedly setting the same parameter value every frame; instead, update only when values change to reduce overhead. If multiple animators exist, ensure the correct Animator is referenced in your script; missing Animator references can silently disable animation updates. For performance problems, review clip lengths and compression settings and avoid using uncompressed, long clips across many characters. Finally, use Play Mode with the Animator window open to watch parameters and state changes live—this is often the fastest way to identify mismatches between expected and actual behavior. Here are the essential concepts to keep in mind. First, the Animator Controller is a visual state machine that orchestrates which animation clips play and when. Second, an Animation Clip is the single motion segment—check Loop Time for cycles you expect to repeat. Third, an Animation State represents a node in the Animator and usually holds one clip or a blend tree. Memorize these basics because they form the foundation of Animator design. Use them as a checklist when building or debugging controllers: do your clips loop, are your states connected correctly, and does the Entry route to your default state? Internalize these three building blocks and you’ll be able to construct reliable animation behaviors and debug issues quickly. Finish with three more concise reminders. First, transitions connect states and use parameter-based conditions and Transition Duration to blend between clips. Keep conditions simple and test timings in Play Mode. Second, Animator parameters—Float, Int, Bool, Trigger—are the interface between your scripts and the Animator. Use the correct type and update parameters sparingly to avoid unnecessary internal work. Third, Has Exit Time controls whether a transition waits for the current clip to reach an exit point; use it for uninterruptible actions and avoid it for regular movement to preserve responsiveness. Use these three checks as a quick debug routine when animations behave unexpectedly: look at conditions, confirm parameter updates, and verify whether Has Exit Time is blocking transitions.
